If it is unavailable, the application falls back to the browser's native speech synthesis. The Spirit of It The most meaningful part of the project is that the “ghost” is not treated as something scary. The spirit guardian represents the way family memories continue to speak through recipes, songs, sayings, places, and small traditions. A question such as: What did Abuela Rosa prepare every November? can bring a stored memory back into the conversation and make the family story feel present again. Anima Memory Vault is designed to feel like lighting a candle: a small act of remembrance that keeps someone’s story from disappearing.

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Anima Memory Vault is a Día de los Muertos-inspired family memory application that preserves oral history through an interactive digital ofrenda.

Users can:

  • Add memories, recipes, traditions, and family stories.
  • Store them in MongoDB Atlas.
  • Ask questions about their family history.
  • Retrieve relevant memories using vector search.
  • Receive answers from a warm ancestor-spirit persona.
  • Listen to responses through ElevenLabs narration or the browser's local speech synthesis.

I interpreted “Ghost in the Machine” as a gentle presence of memory: not a frightening ghost, but a spirit guardian that helps keep family voices, traditions, and stories alive.

Demo

Code

Check Github Code

How I Built It

The application uses:

  • React with Vite for the frontend.
  • Node.js and Express for the backend.
  • MongoDB Atlas Vector Search for memory retrieval.
  • Ollama for local AI inference.
  • gemma2:2b for generating ancestor-spirit responses.
  • nomic-embed-text for converting memories and questions into embeddings.
  • ElevenLabs for optional voice narration.
  • The browser Web Speech API as an offline narration fallback.

The RAG flow works like this:

Family memory
    ↓
nomic-embed-text creates an embedding
    ↓
Embedding is stored in MongoDB Atlas
    ↓
User asks a question
    ↓
The question is embedded
    ↓
MongoDB Vector Search retrieves related memories
    ↓
Retrieved memories are provided to gemma2:2b
    ↓
The spirit guardian generates a grounded answer

The application also supports a local in-memory fallback when MongoDB is not configured, allowing the project to run completely locally during development.

One important design decision was to instruct the model not to invent family history:

If the retrieved memories do not contain the answer, the spirit guardian should say so gently instead of creating facts.

This keeps the responses respectful and grounded in the memories that users actually provided.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation made it possible to build a private, meaningful memory experience using local models instead of sending family stories to a closed AI service by default.

Using Ollama means the core generation and embedding workflow can run locally:

Family memories can remain on the user's machine during development.
The project can work without a paid AI API.
Developers can experiment with different open-weight models.
The retrieval and generation pipeline is transparent and customizable.
The application can fall back gracefully when cloud services are unavailable.
MongoDB Atlas adds persistent vector search, while the local Ollama models provide the intelligence behind the experience.

ElevenLabs is an optional enhancement for more natural narration. If it is unavailable, the application falls back to the browser's native speech synthesis.

The Spirit of It

The most meaningful part of the project is that the “ghost” is not treated as something scary.

The spirit guardian represents the way family memories continue to speak through recipes, songs, sayings, places, and small traditions. A question such as:
What did Abuela Rosa prepare every November?

can bring a stored memory back into the conversation and make the family story feel present again.

Anima Memory Vault is designed to feel like lighting a candle: a small act of remembrance that keeps someone’s story from disappearing.

title: On 21 Nov 2024 Adani fell 22.61%. My model didn't know why, and it wasn't allowed to guess.
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4: Ghost in the Machine In our house, the stock market is dinner-table conversation. And after every truly ugly red day, I hear the same sentence: "Nobody could have seen that coming." I always wanted to ask: how unexpected was it, really? Not "it fell a lot", but how far outside normal it was for that stock , given everything it had done before. So I built something that answers exactly that question. It doesn't read the news. All it knows is a stock's own past. Then I pointed it at 21 November 2024 . That day, Adani Enterprises fell 22.61% . Going in, my model had studied 750 days of the stock's history and drawn the line for a truly terrible day at about −10% . The real day went more than twice as far. The model couldn't say why. It could only say: this day should not have been possible. That's a ghost. I built a machine to hunt them. What I Built Ghost Candles looks back through any Indian stock's history, finds the days its own past could not explain, and gives each one a ghost story. It has two AI models with very different jobs: The Oracle ( TabPFN-3.5 , running on my laptop): for every trading day, it looks only at the days before it and predicts a range of likely moves, like a weather forecast for a stock: "98% sure tomorrow lands between −10% and +9%." The ghosts: if the real move lands far outside that range, with odds of 1 in 100 or worse, the day becomes a Poltergeist . If it breaks past the very edge of the forecast, it's a Wraith . The Medium (Google's Gemma, running locally through Ollama): writes a short ghost story for each one. It gets the numbers and one unbreakable rule: you do not know why this happened, so you may never give a reason. Everything ends up in one web page: a chart with glowing ghosts, a card and story for each, and an honesty check on the Oracle. Demo Click a glowing dot and read its ghost: Adani Enterprises: https://bhaktika.github.io/ghost-candles/out/ADANIENT_NS.html Reliance Industries: https://bhaktika.github.io/ghost-candles/out/RELIANCE_NS.html The night the Wraith walked TabPFN expected 21 November 2024 to land somewhere between −9.92% and +8.98% . It fell 22.61% , on 19.8 times the usual trading volume. I know what happened that day: the group's shares crashed after news that US prosecutors had charged its chairman. The model doesn't know that, and Gemma isn't allowed to guess. Ghost Candles doesn't explain the past. It points at the exact moment an explanation was needed. It happened with Reliance too, two nights in a row: Monday, 3 June 2024: +5.59% . TabPFN rated it 1 in 215. Tuesday, 4 June 2024: −7.49% . TabPFN rated it 1 in 327. Those are the exit-poll rally and the results-day crash of India's 2024 general election. The model has never heard of an election. It just knew both days were wrong. Here's a piece of what Gemma wrote for the Wraith: The candle, a fractured thing of obsidian, plummeted. The model, a pale imitation of prediction, shuddered with an impossibility. The record: -22.61% on 2024-11-21, with a model's odds of approximately 1 in 1,000+ that the move would occur. The story can be dramatic. "The record" line always states the plain facts. The First Reader: Our Dinner Table I showed the live Adani page to the person at our dinner table who trades every day, the one who usually says "nobody could have seen that coming." Here's what they told me (paraphrased): On 21 November 2024: Of course they remembered it. Next to TabPFN's −9.92% to +8.98% range, the real −22.61% made them agree: the model was right to call it impossible. The catch: a seasoned quant would shrug, because ranges built from history always break in a panic. On the quiet 23 July 2026 ghost: Not impressed. Sleepy low-volume dips happen all the time in Indian markets; flag too many and people close the tab. On using it every week: They wouldn't. If your stock falls 22%, you already watched it happen. Unless it warns you before , it's a clever post-mortem. All three are fair. The big ghosts are where it earns its keep: it measures how abnormal a day was, without hindsight, even though it can't say why . Quiet ghosts need a higher bar, so the next version should require a minimum move or a volume spike. And yes, it's a post-mortem; I'm not claiming otherwise. How I Built It 1. Turning candles into a table TabPFN is built for tables, so each trading day becomes one row of 17 columns describing the stock up to the night before : recent returns, how jumpy it had been, how busy trading was, how far it sat from its 50-day average, and so on. That "night before" rule matters most: if the model could see even a hint of the day it's predicting, nothing would look surprising, and there would be no ghosts. 2. Never letting it peek at the future The Oracle learns from the previous 750 trading days, forecasts the next 20, then slides forward: 34 rounds and 671 forecast days per stock, each one a forecast it could really have made at the time. TabPFN makes this cheap. It's pretrained on millions of made-up tables and learns a new table just by reading it, so there's no training and I didn't tune a single setting. With TabPFN-3.5-Fast it ran on my i3 laptop with no GPU : about 11 minutes for Adani, 18 for Reliance. 3. A range, not a single guess This one line is what the whole project stands on: quantiles = model . predict ( X_test , output_type = " quantiles " , quantiles = LEVELS ) Most models give one number: "tomorrow: +0.3%". You can't call a day impossible without knowing what was possible . TabPFN gives the whole spread, from the 0.1% worst case to the 99.9% best case. Where the real day landed in that spread becomes its odds. 4. Can the Oracle be trusted? A ghost detector is only as good as its sense of "normal". If its ranges are too narrow, everything looks haunted. So I compared TabPFN against the textbook shortcut almost everyone uses: assuming daily moves follow a bell curve. Adani Enterprises, 671 forecast days: TabPFN Bell curve Ghosts flagged (pure luck would give about 7) 4 24 Its "98% sure" range actually held 99.0% 95.1% Overall forecast error (lower is better) 34.7 36.5 Reliance Industries, 671 forecast days: TabPFN Bell curve Ghosts flagged (pure luck would give about 7) 5 16 Its "98% sure" range actually held 98.4% 96.4% Overall forecast error (lower is better) 20.3 20.4 In plain words: The bell curve panics. On Adani it shouted "1 in 100!" 24 times, more than three times what luck alone would produce. Its "98% sure" range was really about 95% sure, so it's overconfident exactly where ghosts live. TabPFN stays calm, and is right to. It flagged 4 and 5 ghosts, close to what an honest forecaster should. It wins clearly on the wild stock and only barely on the calm one. On Adani its overall error is about 5% lower. On Reliance it's essentially a tie. It's slightly too careful. Its ranges ran a little wide (99% instead of 98%), so it may miss a ghost rather than invent one. That's the right mistake. It sees things the bell curve can't. On 23 July 2026, Adani dipped 4.37% on a quiet day. The bell curve said 1 in 27; TabPFN, knowing how calm the stock had been, said 1 in 102. (My first reader wasn't convinced that kind of ghost matters. Fair.) 5. The storyteller needed a fact-checker My first storyteller, the tiny gemma3:1b , never invented a reason, but it was terrible with numbers. It turned a +5.26% day into "nearly eight percent" and a −10.65% crash into "a single negative percentage point" . So before any story reaches the page, a small checker reads it and sends it back if it: uses any number that wasn't in the facts it was given, spells a number out in words (which can't be checked), names a possible cause like earnings, an election or news, runs too long, or forgets the plain "The record:" line at the end. Gemma gets three tries. If it still fails, the page shows a plain factual summary instead. Even with the bigger gemma3:4b , the checker rejected 12 of 17 drafts . Many were just too long, but some were sneaky: It invented share prices ("the open price was 188.73, the close 199.33") that appear nowhere in its facts. Told not to write numbers as words, it turned "8.6x normal volume" into "eight hundred and sixty unseen hands" . Gemma wrote 5 of the 9 stories; the other 4 are plain summaries. A boring true sentence beats a spooky false one. 6. The page The journal is one HTML file with no outside scripts, hosted free on GitHub Pages. I used an AI coding assistant to help write and debug the code; every run, number and story here comes from running it myself. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? It's free to run, again and again. Hundreds of model calls across my testing, with no API bill and no rate limits. Your watchlist stays yours. The stocks you look up say a lot about you. Here nothing leaves the laptop. I can open up every part. TabPFN gives me its full range of outcomes. When the small Gemma got numbers wrong, I swapped in a bigger one with one flag and wrapped it in my own checker, and I can read every rejected draft. It can't be switched off. Both models are files on my disk, which felt right for a project about things that refuse to stay dead. Who Could Use This, and How It Would Scale Under the ghost stories is a useful idea: a surprise score for every stock, measured against its own normal . A 3% drop in a sleepy stock can mean more than 6% in a wild one, and a "top losers" list can't tell the difference. Investors could check which holdings did something truly abnormal; analysts could find the strange days first, then read the news for just those; surveillance teams look for exactly the shape of 21 November 2024, a huge unexpected move on heavy volume. My first reader is right that nobody opens a post-mortem weekly. The version worth building is a nightly scan: one forecast per stock ("was today a ghost?") across a watchlist or a whole exchange, with Gemma writing only for the few ghosts. What stands in the way: TabPFN-3.5's weights are non-commercial, so a paid product would need a commercial licence, and two stocks is far too little evidence. What It Isn't Not a trading signal and not financial advice. It tells you a day was strange, not that tomorrow will be. Moves past the forecast's edge show as "1 in 1,000+", not a precise number the model can't back up. Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine . The Oracle: TabPFN-3.5 , an open-weight tabular foundation model, runs locally. summary_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

In our house, the stock market is dinner-table conversation. And after every truly ugly red day, I hear the same sentence:

"Nobody could have seen that coming."

I always wanted to ask: how unexpected was it, really? Not "it fell a lot", but how far outside normal it was for that stock, given everything it had done before.

So I built something that answers exactly that question. It doesn't read the news. All it knows is a stock's own past.

Then I pointed it at 21 November 2024.

That day, Adani Enterprises fell 22.61%. Going in, my model had studied 750 days of the stock's history and drawn the line for a truly terrible day at about −10%. The real day went more than twice as far. The model couldn't say why. It could only say: this day should not have been possible.

That's a ghost. I built a machine to hunt them.

What I Built

Ghost Candles looks back through any Indian stock's history, finds the days its own past could not explain, and gives each one a ghost story.

It has two AI models with very different jobs:

  • The Oracle (TabPFN-3.5, running on my laptop): for every trading day, it looks only at the days before it and predicts a range of likely moves, like a weather forecast for a stock: "98% sure tomorrow lands between −10% and +9%."
  • The ghosts: if the real move lands far outside that range, with odds of 1 in 100 or worse, the day becomes a Poltergeist. If it breaks past the very edge of the forecast, it's a Wraith.
  • The Medium (Google's Gemma, running locally through Ollama): writes a short ghost story for each one. It gets the numbers and one unbreakable rule: you do not know why this happened, so you may never give a reason.

Everything ends up in one web page: a chart with glowing ghosts, a card and story for each, and an honesty check on the Oracle.

Demo

Click a glowing dot and read its ghost:

  • Adani Enterprises: https://bhaktika.github.io/ghost-candles/out/ADANIENT_NS.html
  • Reliance Industries: https://bhaktika.github.io/ghost-candles/out/RELIANCE_NS.html

The night the Wraith walked

TabPFN expected 21 November 2024 to land somewhere between −9.92% and +8.98%. It fell 22.61%, on 19.8 times the usual trading volume.

I know what happened that day: the group's shares crashed after news that US prosecutors had charged its chairman. The model doesn't know that, and Gemma isn't allowed to guess. Ghost Candles doesn't explain the past. It points at the exact moment an explanation was needed.

It happened with Reliance too, two nights in a row:

  • Monday, 3 June 2024: +5.59%. TabPFN rated it 1 in 215.
  • Tuesday, 4 June 2024: −7.49%. TabPFN rated it 1 in 327.

Those are the exit-poll rally and the results-day crash of India's 2024 general election. The model has never heard of an election. It just knew both days were wrong.

Here's a piece of what Gemma wrote for the Wraith:

The candle, a fractured thing of obsidian, plummeted. The model, a pale imitation of prediction, shuddered with an impossibility.

The record: -22.61% on 2024-11-21, with a model's odds of approximately 1 in 1,000+ that the move would occur.

The story can be dramatic. "The record" line always states the plain facts.

The First Reader: Our Dinner Table

I showed the live Adani page to the person at our dinner table who trades every day, the one who usually says "nobody could have seen that coming." Here's what they told me (paraphrased):

  • On 21 November 2024: Of course they remembered it. Next to TabPFN's −9.92% to +8.98% range, the real −22.61% made them agree: the model was right to call it impossible. The catch: a seasoned quant would shrug, because ranges built from history always break in a panic.
  • On the quiet 23 July 2026 ghost: Not impressed. Sleepy low-volume dips happen all the time in Indian markets; flag too many and people close the tab.
  • On using it every week: They wouldn't. If your stock falls 22%, you already watched it happen. Unless it warns you before, it's a clever post-mortem.

All three are fair. The big ghosts are where it earns its keep: it measures how abnormal a day was, without hindsight, even though it can't say why. Quiet ghosts need a higher bar, so the next version should require a minimum move or a volume spike. And yes, it's a post-mortem; I'm not claiming otherwise.

How I Built It 1. Turning candles into a table

TabPFN is built for tables, so each trading day becomes one row of 17 columns describing the stock up to the night before: recent returns, how jumpy it had been, how busy trading was, how far it sat from its 50-day average, and so on. That "night before" rule matters most: if the model could see even a hint of the day it's predicting, nothing would look surprising, and there would be no ghosts.

2. Never letting it peek at the future

The Oracle learns from the previous 750 trading days, forecasts the next 20, then slides forward: 34 rounds and 671 forecast days per stock, each one a forecast it could really have made at the time.

TabPFN makes this cheap. It's pretrained on millions of made-up tables and learns a new table just by reading it, so there's no training and I didn't tune a single setting. With TabPFN-3.5-Fast it ran on my i3 laptop with no GPU: about 11 minutes for Adani, 18 for Reliance.

3. A range, not a single guess

This one line is what the whole project stands on:

quantiles = model.predict(X_test, output_type="quantiles", quantiles=LEVELS)

Most models give one number: "tomorrow: +0.3%". You can't call a day impossible without knowing what was possible. TabPFN gives the whole spread, from the 0.1% worst case to the 99.9% best case. Where the real day landed in that spread becomes its odds.

4. Can the Oracle be trusted?

A ghost detector is only as good as its sense of "normal". If its ranges are too narrow, everything looks haunted. So I compared TabPFN against the textbook shortcut almost everyone uses: assuming daily moves follow a bell curve.

Adani Enterprises, 671 forecast days:

TabPFN Bell curve Ghosts flagged (pure luck would give about 7) 4 24 Its "98% sure" range actually held 99.0% 95.1% Overall forecast error (lower is better) 34.7 36.5

Reliance Industries, 671 forecast days:

TabPFN Bell curve Ghosts flagged (pure luck would give about 7) 5 16 Its "98% sure" range actually held 98.4% 96.4% Overall forecast error (lower is better) 20.3 20.4

In plain words:

  • The bell curve panics. On Adani it shouted "1 in 100!" 24 times, more than three times what luck alone would produce. Its "98% sure" range was really about 95% sure, so it's overconfident exactly where ghosts live.
  • TabPFN stays calm, and is right to. It flagged 4 and 5 ghosts, close to what an honest forecaster should.
  • It wins clearly on the wild stock and only barely on the calm one. On Adani its overall error is about 5% lower. On Reliance it's essentially a tie.
  • It's slightly too careful. Its ranges ran a little wide (99% instead of 98%), so it may miss a ghost rather than invent one. That's the right mistake.
  • It sees things the bell curve can't. On 23 July 2026, Adani dipped 4.37% on a quiet day. The bell curve said 1 in 27; TabPFN, knowing how calm the stock had been, said 1 in 102. (My first reader wasn't convinced that kind of ghost matters. Fair.)
5. The storyteller needed a fact-checker

My first storyteller, the tiny gemma3:1b, never invented a reason, but it was terrible with numbers. It turned a +5.26% day into "nearly eight percent" and a −10.65% crash into "a single negative percentage point".

So before any story reaches the page, a small checker reads it and sends it back if it:

  • uses any number that wasn't in the facts it was given,
  • spells a number out in words (which can't be checked),
  • names a possible cause like earnings, an election or news,
  • runs too long, or
  • forgets the plain "The record:" line at the end.

Gemma gets three tries. If it still fails, the page shows a plain factual summary instead.

Even with the bigger gemma3:4b, the checker rejected 12 of 17 drafts. Many were just too long, but some were sneaky:

  • It invented share prices ("the open price was 188.73, the close 199.33") that appear nowhere in its facts.
  • Told not to write numbers as words, it turned "8.6x normal volume" into "eight hundred and sixty unseen hands".

Gemma wrote 5 of the 9 stories; the other 4 are plain summaries. A boring true sentence beats a spooky false one.

6. The page

The journal is one HTML file with no outside scripts, hosted free on GitHub Pages. I used an AI coding assistant to help write and debug the code; every run, number and story here comes from running it myself.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

It's free to run, again and again. Hundreds of model calls across my testing, with no API bill and no rate limits.

Your watchlist stays yours. The stocks you look up say a lot about you. Here nothing leaves the laptop.

I can open up every part. TabPFN gives me its full range of outcomes. When the small Gemma got numbers wrong, I swapped in a bigger one with one flag and wrapped it in my own checker, and I can read every rejected draft.

It can't be switched off. Both models are files on my disk, which felt right for a project about things that refuse to stay dead.

Who Could Use This, and How It Would Scale

Under the ghost stories is a useful idea: a surprise score for every stock, measured against its own normal. A 3% drop in a sleepy stock can mean more than 6% in a wild one, and a "top losers" list can't tell the difference. Investors could check which holdings did something truly abnormal; analysts could find the strange days first, then read the news for just those; surveillance teams look for exactly the shape of 21 November 2024, a huge unexpected move on heavy volume.

My first reader is right that nobody opens a post-mortem weekly. The version worth building is a nightly scan: one forecast per stock ("was today a ghost?") across a watchlist or a whole exchange, with Gemma writing only for the few ghosts.

What stands in the way: TabPFN-3.5's weights are non-commercial, so a paid product would need a commercial licence, and two stocks is far too little evidence.

What It Isn't

Not a trading signal and not financial advice. It tells you a day was strange, not that tomorrow will be. Moves past the forecast's edge show as "1 in 1,000+", not a precise number the model can't back up.

title: Wraith: a ghost in my zsh that stops your hand before the dangerous command runs
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built $ git push --force origin main ╭─ the wraith bars the door ─────────────────────────────────╮ │ git push --force origin main │ │ │ │ Force-pushing to a shared branch rewrites history that │ │ other people already have. │ │ │ │ ☾ I will wait. title: AWS Kiro Core: Building Smarter Applications with Agentic Development
summary: AI coding tools are changing how developers build software. Today, we can ask AI to generate functions, explain errors, create APIs, write tests, and even help build complete applications. But there is one important problem: generating code does not automatically mean building good software. A reliable application still needs clear requirements, proper architecture, consistent coding standards, security, testing, and maintainability. This is where AWS Kiro becomes interesting. Kiro is an agentic development environment from AWS that helps developers go beyond simple AI code generation. It introduces structured development workflows through specifications, steering documents, agent hooks, MCP integrations, and specialized agent capabilities. Instead of simply asking AI to write code, developers can guide an agent through understanding a project, defining requirements, designing a solution, implementing features, and validating the results. In this article, we'll explore AWS Kiro Core, understand its most useful capabilities, and build a practical Student Management Portal feature using a hands-on approach. 1. What Is AWS Kiro? AWS Kiro is an agentic integrated development environment designed to help developers build and maintain software with AI assistance. Traditional AI coding assistants generally focus on answering questions, generating code snippets, and completing code. Kiro takes a broader approach by supporting different stages of software development. Imagine that you want to add a student search feature to an existing application. You might initially ask: Add a search feature to my Student Management Portal. But several questions remain: Should users search by name, email, or student ID? Should the feature support filters? How should pagination work? Which APIs need to change? What validation is required? How should authorization work? Which automated tests should be added? Kiro helps developers approach these questions systematically. A simplified agentic development workflow looks like this: Business Requirement | v Requirements | v Technical Design | v Implementation Tasks | v Code Generation | v Testing & Review | v Working Feature The key idea is to understand the problem before implementing the solution. 2. Core AWS Kiro Capabilities Let's explore the capabilities that make Kiro useful for modern software engineering. 2.1 Spec-Driven Development One of Kiro's most interesting capabilities is spec-driven development. In many AI coding workflows, developers provide a prompt and immediately receive generated code. That approach can work for small tasks, but larger features need proper planning. Spec-driven development introduces a structured process before implementation. A typical specification contains three important artifacts. requirements.md Describes what needs to be built. It can include: User stories. Functional requirements. Acceptance criteria. Expected application behavior. Validation requirements. design.md Describes how the feature should be implemented. It may include: Application architecture. Database changes. API design. Component responsibilities. Security considerations. Technical decisions. tasks.md Breaks implementation into manageable development tasks. Example: Student Search Feature 1. Review the existing student model. 2. Review the current student API. 3. Add search functionality. 4. Add course filtering. 5. Add enrollment status filtering. 6. Implement pagination. 7. Add input validation. 8. Write automated tests. 9. Verify existing functionality. The developer can review these files, correct requirements, and approve the plan before implementation begins. Why is this useful? It reduces ambiguity and gives developers more control over what the agent is going to build. Rather than discovering missing requirements after code generation, teams can identify them during planning. 2.2 Steering Documents One common problem with AI coding assistants is repeatedly explaining the same project details. AI coding tools are changing how developers build software.

Today, we can ask AI to generate functions, explain errors, create APIs, write tests, and even help build complete applications.

But there is one important problem: generating code does not automatically mean building good software.

A reliable application still needs clear requirements, proper architecture, consistent coding standards, security, testing, and maintainability.

This is where AWS Kiro becomes interesting.

Kiro is an agentic development environment from AWS that helps developers go beyond simple AI code generation. It introduces structured development workflows through specifications, steering documents, agent hooks, MCP integrations, and specialized agent capabilities.

Instead of simply asking AI to write code, developers can guide an agent through understanding a project, defining requirements, designing a solution, implementing features, and validating the results.

In this article, we'll explore AWS Kiro Core, understand its most useful capabilities, and build a practical Student Management Portal feature using a hands-on approach.

1. What Is AWS Kiro?

AWS Kiro is an agentic integrated development environment designed to help developers build and maintain software with AI assistance.

Traditional AI coding assistants generally focus on answering questions, generating code snippets, and completing code.

Kiro takes a broader approach by supporting different stages of software development.

Imagine that you want to add a student search feature to an existing application.

You might initially ask:

Add a search feature to my
Student Management Portal.

But several questions remain:

  • Should users search by name, email, or student ID?
  • Should the feature support filters?
  • How should pagination work?
  • Which APIs need to change?
  • What validation is required?
  • How should authorization work?
  • Which automated tests should be added?

Kiro helps developers approach these questions systematically.

A simplified agentic development workflow looks like this:

       Business Requirement
                |
                v
          Requirements
                |
                v
          Technical Design
                |
                v
        Implementation Tasks
                |
                v
          Code Generation
                |
                v
          Testing & Review
                |
                v
          Working Feature

The key idea is to understand the problem before implementing the solution.

2. Core AWS Kiro Capabilities

Let's explore the capabilities that make Kiro useful for modern software engineering.

2.1 Spec-Driven Development

One of Kiro's most interesting capabilities is spec-driven development.

In many AI coding workflows, developers provide a prompt and immediately receive generated code.

That approach can work for small tasks, but larger features need proper planning.

Spec-driven development introduces a structured process before implementation.

A typical specification contains three important artifacts.

requirements.md

Describes what needs to be built.

It can include:

  • User stories.
  • Functional requirements.
  • Acceptance criteria.
  • Expected application behavior.
  • Validation requirements.

design.md

Describes how the feature should be implemented.

It may include:

  • Application architecture.
  • Database changes.
  • API design.
  • Component responsibilities.
  • Security considerations.
  • Technical decisions.

tasks.md

Breaks implementation into manageable development tasks.

Example:

Student Search Feature

1. Review the existing student model.
2. Review the current student API.
3. Add search functionality.
4. Add course filtering.
5. Add enrollment status filtering.
6. Implement pagination.
7. Add input validation.
8. Write automated tests.
9. Verify existing functionality.

The developer can review these files, correct requirements, and approve the plan before implementation begins.

Why is this useful?

It reduces ambiguity and gives developers more control over what the agent is going to build.

Rather than discovering missing requirements after code generation, teams can identify them during planning.

2.2 Steering Documents

One common problem with AI coding assistants is repeatedly explaining the same project details.

For example:

  • Which programming language does the project use?
  • Which framework is being used?
  • What database is configured?
  • What coding standards should be followed?
  • Where should new files be created?
  • How should errors be handled?

Kiro uses steering documents to provide persistent project-specific guidance.

A typical project structure looks like this:

my-application/
│
├── frontend/
├── backend/
├── tests/
│
└── .kiro/
    └── steering/
        ├── product.md
        ├── tech.md
        └── structure.md

Example tech.md:

# Technology Standards

- Backend: Python FastAPI
- Frontend: React
- Database: PostgreSQL
- API architecture: REST
- Testing framework: Pytest

# Development Guidelines

- Follow existing project conventions.
- Validate user inputs.
- Use environment variables for configuration.
- Never hardcode credentials.
- Write automated tests for new features.
- Avoid unnecessary dependencies.
- Follow least-privilege security principles.

Steering documents should describe the actual project rather than introducing technologies that the application does not use.

Productivity benefit: Developers spend less time repeating project instructions, and AI-generated changes can follow established development standards more consistently.

2.3 Agent Hooks

Developers frequently perform repetitive activities:

  • Running tests after modifying code.
  • Checking coding standards.
  • Reviewing changes.
  • Updating documentation.
  • Validating configuration files.

Kiro Hooks can help automate development activities based on configured events.

Example workflow:

Developer Changes Code
          |
          v
       Agent Hook
          |
          v
     Run Test Command
          |
          v
     Review Test Results
          |
          v
    Developer Reviews Fixes

For example, you can configure a workflow that runs relevant backend tests after backend files are modified.

Hooks can reduce manual effort and help developers maintain consistent workflows.

However, automation should be configured carefully. Running tests is generally low risk, while deploying code or modifying production infrastructure requires stronger safeguards.

2.4 Model Context Protocol (MCP)

The Model Context Protocol, commonly called MCP, provides a standardized way for AI agents to interact with external tools and services through configured MCP servers.

This is useful because developers often need information outside their local codebase.

For example, when developing an AWS application, you might need to:

  • Find AWS service documentation.
  • Understand an API operation.
  • Check configuration requirements.
  • Investigate integration problems.
  • Access connected developer tools.

With an appropriately configured MCP server, Kiro can interact with supported external tools and retrieve relevant information.

The AWS Documentation MCP server is particularly useful for AWS-related development workflows.

Research the best AWS services for deploying
this application.

2. Deployment architecture.
3. Security considerations.
4. Networking requirements.
5. Cost considerations.
6. Monitoring and logging options.

Use the available AWS documentation tools.

Do not create or deploy AWS resources.
Only provide a technical recommendation.

MCP does not automatically grant unrestricted access to external systems. Available tools and permissions depend on the server configuration and the permissions granted to the agent.

3. Review specifications before implementation.

An incorrect requirement can produce incorrect code. Review the requirements and design before proceeding.

4. Keep steering documents updated.

Outdated technical context can lead to incorrect implementation decisions.

5. Automate repetitive tasks.

Use hooks for routine checks, but keep risky operations under developer control.

6. Apply least-privilege access.

Do not give agents unrestricted access to production environments, credentials, or cloud resources.

7. Test AI-generated code.

Run unit tests, integration tests, security checks, and application-level validation.

8. Review every important change.

Inspect code diffs, dependency changes, infrastructure modifications, and deployment plans.

9. Protect sensitive information.

Never expose API keys, database passwords, access tokens, or confidential application data in prompts or project documentation.

10. Keep humans involved in important decisions.

AI agents can accelerate engineering work, but developers remain responsible for architecture, security, quality, and production readiness.

8. Final Thoughts

AWS Kiro represents an important direction in AI-assisted software engineering.

The real opportunity is not simply asking AI to generate more code. It is using an agent that understands project context, helps define requirements, follows development standards, connects with useful tools, and supports repeatable engineering workflows.

🧩 What I Built

Healthcare information is dangerously fragmented across short consultations, handwritten prescriptions, laboratory documents, hospital discharge papers, and specialist referrals.

To bridge these gaps, I built Diagnosia: a connected healthcare workflow platform that helps clinicians, specialists, patients, and care teams manage information across the entire patient journey.

Diagnosia is not a collection of disconnected AI demos. It is a coordinated system where:

  1. 📥 Information enters through existing workflows
  2. 🤖 AI prepares reviewable drafts
  3. 🔐 Authorized modules reuse relevant context
  4. 🔄 Workflow events update the patient journey
🛠️ Core Tools

The platform is anchored by three foundational tools:

Tool Purpose 🎙️ DiagnoFast Voice-first patient intake 🔬 Skin Cancer Detection Image-based screening support 💊 Prescription Analyzer Medication interpretation
➕ Add-On Modules

Four focused modules extend this foundation:

Module Purpose 📝 ClinScribe Encounter summarization 🧪 LabLens Lab report digitisation 🏥 DischargeCare Transition coordination 🔁 ReferralLoop Specialist tracking
🎬 Demo

📂 View the demo folder on Google Drive

The platform's visual identity reflects its underlying clarity, as shown in the UI screenshots in the demo folder.

  1. 🎙️ DiagnoFast captures a voice interview and queues a report
  2. 🧪 LabLens digitises a scanned test
  3. 📝 ClinScribe drafts a clinical note based entirely on the consultation transcript
  4. ⚡ The timeline updates live, without reloading, reflecting every state change
🤝 Partner Technologies

Three sponsor technologies were integrated, each with a strictly defined, isolated responsibility to prevent conflicting sources of truth.

Partner Role Responsibility ✨ Google Gemini API Multimodal engine Reads scanned lab reports and prescription photos; outputs are validated against a schema before reaching human review 🗄️ YugabyteDB Technical audit trail Holds all records of AI runs, attempts, and handoffs, keeping the core clinical database clean 🧠 Meko (via MCP server) Shared agent context Manages approved knowledge and memory 🍃 MongoDB Atlas Workflow event store Uses Change Streams to instantly project updates onto open care screens
🏗️ Architecture Principles
  • One responsibility per technology: no sponsor database may override the local identity authority
  • Schema-validated AI output: nothing reaches a reviewer unchecked
  • Event-driven timeline: state changes are projected live via Change Streams
  • Context reuse by authorization: modules only access relevant, permitted context
  • Audit separated from clinical data: technical records never pollute the core clinical database
🔒 Safety Boundaries
  • ✅ Synthetic data only: this is a pilot, not a clinical product
  • ✅ AI output = draft: never final until approved by an authorized human reviewer
  • ✅ Local identity authority is the single source of truth for identity
  • ✅ Schema validation on all multimodal AI outputs
  • ✅ Full audit trail of every AI run, attempt, and handoff
💭 Hackathon Experience

Building a modular, feature-frozen product with strict safety boundaries was an incredible test of technical discipline.

Wrangling the architecture so that no sponsor database overrode our local identity authority taught me a core lesson:

Building for healthcare isn't just about moving fast. It is about meticulously engineering trust.

Diagnosia · Connected care, reviewable by design.

title: How We Built Metis in 7 Hours: Recovering Hidden Decisions from Open-Source Projects
summary: Hackathons are exciting, but the real experience begins when you have to turn an idea into something that actually works. When Hacktoberfest Hack Day started, I was nervous. I wanted to build something meaningful, but choosing the right problem statement felt like the first challenge. After listening to talks from four champions, my excitement grew. Their experiences reminded me that hackathons are about learning, experimenting, and pushing yourself beyond what you already know. At around 6:30 PM, our team, Dot, started exploring the problem statements. After nearly an hour of discussion, we selected Problem Statement 6: Open Source Decision Intelligence and Knowledge Recovery. That decision became the starting point of Mentis. The Problem We Wanted to Solve Open-source projects accumulate years of development activity across GitHub commits, pull requests, issues, and code changes. Among this activity are important updates and changes to the codebase, but keeping track of them can become difficult. Imagine a developer making changes to a parser, improving its performance, fixing bugs, or modifying an existing implementation. After the changes are tested and verified, the commit becomes part of the project's development history. However, understanding what changed and keeping track of verified commits across a repository can still be challenging. As projects grow, developers need a reliable way to monitor commits that have already been verified and understand the changes they represent. Without an organized way to track this information, important updates can become difficult to follow. The problem isn't that developers lack information. It's that keeping track of valuable, verified code changes becomes difficult as repositories grow. We wanted to make that information easier to monitor and access. Introducing Mentis Our team, Dot, decided to build Mentis, a project designed to help developers monitor GitHub commits that have already been verified. The goal was to make it easier to track verified commits from GitHub instead of manually searching through repository activity. We wanted Mentis to help answer one important question: What verified changes have been made to this repository? It was an interesting challenge because it combined repository analysis, information retrieval, backend development, and AI. Building the Product Our tech stack included: Frontend: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS Backend: Python, FastAPI REST API Database: PostgreSQL We chose this stack to build a full-stack application with a frontend for interacting with Mentis, a REST API for backend communication, and PostgreSQL for structured data storage. Development rarely followed a straight path. We researched the problem, analyzed the repository, explored suitable libraries, and worked on connecting the different components. The frontend needed to communicate with the backend, the backend needed to handle application logic, and the database had to support the information we were working with. With limited time, we focused on the essential parts of the product rather than trying to perfect every feature. The AI Integration Challenge One challenge came during AI integration. We wanted the AI to work with repository information, but it wasn't fetching the backend code as expected. That meant the AI was missing important context required for analysis. It taught us a lesson that sounds simple but matters in real applications: An AI model cannot analyze code that the application has not successfully retrieved and provided. Adding AI is not just about writing a prompt. The entire data flow matters—from accessing repository information to passing the right context into the model. The experience showed us that an AI-powered product depends just as much on reliable backend communication and data retrieval as it does on the model itself. The Midnight Journey As the night progressed, excitement slowly turned into exhaustion. The clock kept moving. Our screens were still open, tasks were unfinished, and the deadline was getting closer. After hours of staring at code and debugging, even simple problems started demanding more concentration. There were moments when we felt completely drained. But whenever we looked at the progress we had made, it reminded us why we were still there. We kept working—fixing problems, making improvements, and bringing the different pieces together. Then came 5:30 AM. After nearly seven hours of work, we finally merged our PR. That moment felt different. It wasn't just another GitHub notification. It represented hours of research, coding, debugging, and teamwork. We had started the evening unsure which problem to choose. Now, we had a product ready to submit. We were exhausted, but seeing our work come together made every hour feel worth it. We submitted Mentis. For a moment, there was relief. The product was in, and we had reached the goal we had been working toward. But the hackathon wasn't over. We shifted straight into presentation preparation. Now we had to explain the problem, demonstrate what we built, and communicate why Mentis mattered. After a night of writing code, we were preparing to tell the story behind it. What I Took Away Hacktoberfest Hack Day taught me that building a product is about much more than implementation. Choosing the right problem, researching the repository, connecting technologies, and working through unexpected failures are all part of development. The AI integration challenge reminded me to understand the complete data pipeline before expecting meaningful results. And the overnight journey showed me what persistence looks like when a deadline is approaching. We started with uncertainty, built Mentis, merged our PR at 5:30 AM, submitted the product, and moved on to preparing our presentation. It wasn't a perfect journey, but it was a real one. At 6:30 PM, we had a problem statement. At 5:30 AM, we had a product. And somewhere between those hours, Team Dot learned what it takes to turn an idea into reality.

title: Lumbre: a Día de los Muertos altar that only remembers what you tell it
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built Lumbre is a small altar for Día de los Muertos. You write the name of someone you want to remember, how you knew them, the years if you know them, one memory, and any food, song, or object that belongs with them. An open-weight model writes the line that sits on the altar and a short remembrance. The memory you typed is kept word for word, under "As told." The food, the song, and the object come from the form. A field you leave blank stays blank. The model is told not to invent a date, a relative, or a favorite thing you did not give it. I read the week as remembrance rather than a jump scare. Día de los Muertos is the thin place between someone who is gone and the people who still set a place for them. title: A ChatGPT share link leaked your private conversations
summary: In October 2026, a research team at parameter.ai turned an ordinary public ChatGPT share link into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it. The victim only had to open the link. There was no app to install, no project to join, no code to paste, no developer tools. OpenAI classified the report as P1 and shipped a fix on October 26. The payload ran as chatgpt.com, which is the part that matters. From there it enumerated the victim's conversation list, pulled the content of a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and sent selected data to an external server. It called ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, so its reach was whatever the normal frontend can do on your account. The chain is worth walking through because no single piece of it was broken. A graph and a preview ChatGPT's Preview feature renders an HTML code block as a working page. Since that HTML can contain anything, ChatGPT runs it inside a restricted frame on a separate web address. The browser treats the Preview as a different site, so code inside it cannot read parent.document or otherwise inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it. That isolation held. Preview code could not reach the parent directly. The same conversation also contained an interactive graph. Rendering it loaded a math library, MathLive. Loading MathLive did one extra thing: it installed a postMessage listener in the main ChatGPT page to handle its on-screen keyboard. postMessage is the sanctioned way for two frames to talk when the browser won't let them read each other's pages. It is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message. MathLive's top-level controller used an origin policy of none, so it accepted messages from any origin, and it did not require the setting-change message to come from a window it had previously approved. The graph installed the receiver; the sandboxed Preview supplied a sender nobody had vetted. HTML into the parent The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual-keyboard layout with the attacker's HTML, since MathLive allowed keyboard layouts to contain raw markup. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, which joined the layout into an HTML string and assigned it to innerHTML in the real ChatGPT page. A helper called createHTML looked like it might sanitize that string. It was an identity Trusted Types wrapper: it marked the string as trusted and passed it through unchanged. Trusted Types can control who writes to an HTML sink, but an identity policy doesn't make an attacker's string safe. innerHTML alone doesn't execute script; tags injected that way stay inert. The layout therefore inserted an iframe with a srcdoc attribute, and MathLive added that frame to the main document with no sandbox attribute. srcdoc forces a fresh HTML parse, which gives an external script somewhere to run, and because the main chatgpt.com page created the frame, the browser handed the new document the chatgpt.com origin. Code inside it could now read the parent. Getting script past CSP Content Security Policy blocked inline JavaScript, as it should. It did allow scripts from YouTube. YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supports a JSONP-style callback parameter, and JSONP responses are JavaScript, not JSON. The endpoint rejected invalid callbacks, but it wrote the callback into the response body before appending its validation error. Ending the callback with ;void turned the trailing error object into a no-op. The response came back HTTP 200 with Content-Type text/javascript and nosniff set, and since YouTube was on the CSP allowlist, the browser loaded it as a script and ran the callback inside the unsandboxed frame. That produced arbitrary JavaScript executing as chatgpt.com. Google rewrites angle brackets in the callback, so the payload used classic function syntax rather than arrow functions to survive the round trip. From lab bug to one link The first working version used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the message sender, which meant a victim would have to connect or invoke that app first. A native HTML attachment removed that step, since ChatGPT opened the attachment in the same sandboxed Preview. But exporting the conversation as a public share kept the attachment and dropped the graph, and the graph was what loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable listener. The attachment could still send the two messages, but nothing in the parent was listening. The working approach put both halves in one ordinary public conversation: a genuine graph to initialize MathLive in the main page, and a later assistant-authored HTML Preview to send the messages. The resulting /share/ link carried the whole chain to anyone who opened it, deliverable by email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post. Because the graph and Preview loaded independently, the payload sometimes fired before MathLive was ready, so the carrier retried the two messages for a short window, with a guard in the parent so the data-theft step ran only once. In the most stable reproduction the victim clicked Preview once; marking the HTML block as previewable made ChatGPT open it automatically, reducing the whole thing to a single click on the link. The automatic path reproduced three times in a separate account, including after a hard refresh, with the proof alert appearing around 4.5 seconds in. What the code actually did An alert proves where code runs, not why it matters. The same-origin frame parsed #client-bootstrap out of the parent document, pulled the session access token and account ID, and checked that the account ID in the token matched the session when both were present. In October 2026, a research team at parameter.ai turned an ordinary public ChatGPT share link into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it. The victim only had to open the link. There was no app to install, no project to join, no code to paste, no developer tools. OpenAI classified the report as P1 and shipped a fix on October 26.

The payload ran as chatgpt.com, which is the part that matters. From there it enumerated the victim's conversation list, pulled the content of a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and sent selected data to an external server. It called ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, so its reach was whatever the normal frontend can do on your account.

The chain is worth walking through because no single piece of it was broken.

A graph and a preview

ChatGPT's Preview feature renders an HTML code block as a working page. Since that HTML can contain anything, ChatGPT runs it inside a restricted frame on a separate web address. The browser treats the Preview as a different site, so code inside it cannot read parent.document or otherwise inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it. That isolation held. Preview code could not reach the parent directly.

The same conversation also contained an interactive graph. Rendering it loaded a math library, MathLive. Loading MathLive did one extra thing: it installed a postMessage listener in the main ChatGPT page to handle its on-screen keyboard.

postMessage is the sanctioned way for two frames to talk when the browser won't let them read each other's pages. It is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message. MathLive's top-level controller used an origin policy of none, so it accepted messages from any origin, and it did not require the setting-change message to come from a window it had previously approved. The graph installed the receiver; the sandboxed Preview supplied a sender nobody had vetted.

HTML into the parent

The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual-keyboard layout with the attacker's HTML, since MathLive allowed keyboard layouts to contain raw markup. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, which joined the layout into an HTML string and assigned it to innerHTML in the real ChatGPT page. A helper called createHTML looked like it might sanitize that string. It was an identity Trusted Types wrapper: it marked the string as trusted and passed it through unchanged. Trusted Types can control who writes to an HTML sink, but an identity policy doesn't make an attacker's string safe.

innerHTML alone doesn't execute script; tags injected that way stay inert. The layout therefore inserted an iframe with a srcdoc attribute, and MathLive added that frame to the main document with no sandbox attribute. srcdoc forces a fresh HTML parse, which gives an external script somewhere to run, and because the main chatgpt.com page created the frame, the browser handed the new document the chatgpt.com origin. Code inside it could now read the parent.

Getting script past CSP

Content Security Policy blocked inline JavaScript, as it should. It did allow scripts from YouTube. YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supports a JSONP-style callback parameter, and JSONP responses are JavaScript, not JSON. The endpoint rejected invalid callbacks, but it wrote the callback into the response body before appending its validation error. Ending the callback with ;void turned the trailing error object into a no-op. The response came back HTTP 200 with Content-Type text/javascript and nosniff set, and since YouTube was on the CSP allowlist, the browser loaded it as a script and ran the callback inside the unsandboxed frame.

That produced arbitrary JavaScript executing as chatgpt.com. Google rewrites angle brackets in the callback, so the payload used classic function syntax rather than arrow functions to survive the round trip.

From lab bug to one link

The first working version used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the message sender, which meant a victim would have to connect or invoke that app first. A native HTML attachment removed that step, since ChatGPT opened the attachment in the same sandboxed Preview. But exporting the conversation as a public share kept the attachment and dropped the graph, and the graph was what loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable listener. The attachment could still send the two messages, but nothing in the parent was listening.

The working approach put both halves in one ordinary public conversation: a genuine graph to initialize MathLive in the main page, and a later assistant-authored HTML Preview to send the messages. The resulting /share/ link carried the whole chain to anyone who opened it, deliverable by email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post.

Because the graph and Preview loaded independently, the payload sometimes fired before MathLive was ready, so the carrier retried the two messages for a short window, with a guard in the parent so the data-theft step ran only once. In the most stable reproduction the victim clicked Preview once; marking the HTML block as previewable made ChatGPT open it automatically, reducing the whole thing to a single click on the link. title: I built a coroner for dead software. It issues death certificates, and it refuses to lie.
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine Every developer has a graveyard. Mine is a GitHub account full of repos that stopped one day and never started again. A linter I was sure would take off. A "weekend" game engine. Three different note-taking apps, because apparently the first two taught me nothing. I don't delete any of them, because deleting would mean admitting something. So they just sit there with a last commit from some Tuesday, going quietly from green to grey. So for Ghost in the Machine, I built the thing those repos deserve. A coroner. What I Built Autopsy of a Dead Project is a forensic pathology tool for software. You paste a GitHub URL, and a machine examines the body, says plainly what the project was , works out how it died, and issues a death certificate : cause of death, time since the last sign of life, a differential diagnosis, and the project's recovered last words. If the repo turns out to be alive, you get a certificate of LIFE instead, flatline still beating green. I shipped it this week on purpose. It lands on Halloween night and the first hours of Día de los Muertos, and Día de los Muertos isn't about fear. It's about remembering the dead by name. The coroner doesn't mock your abandoned projects, it memorializes them, and it does it with a cause of death it can actually defend. Every certificate recovers what the project was, in plain words, before it ever says how it ended. You're meant to feel something reading it, the way you're meant to feel something at an ofrenda. It's spooky, and it's a little sad, which felt exactly right. Demo A 90-second autopsy, start to finish. Three real repos: one abandoned, one burned out, one still breathing. Try it live: autopsy.132-145-100-81.sslip.io Paste bower/bower , sindresorhus/caprine , or fastapi/fastapi for an instant cached verdict, or feed it one of your own dead repos and wait for the full cold autopsy. The coroner runs on open weights precisely so a vendor can't abandon it the way we abandoned the repos it examines. The graveyard keeper should outlive the graveyard. I'll be exact about one thing, because a coroner that fudges its own architecture has no business lecturing anyone about honesty. TabPFN runs local. The narration and tie-breaking run on 0G Compute, which is a network call, not a local process. There's a fully-local fallback that points the same code at a local Ollama model, but the live demo isn't running it, so I'm not going to pretend it is. Are the weights open end to end? Yes. Does nothing phone home? Not for the live service, and the certificate says so. Every result carries an engine label ( classified by TabPFN , tabpfn + llm · adjudicated , or a plain rules fallback), and the narration badge reads "evidence read by deepseek-v4.1-flash · 0G Compute" , pulled from the real engine field, never hardcoded. Nothing hides behind a generic "AI says." The Spirit of It Here's the design decision I think actually makes this worth shipping. A eulogy is generative text, and generative text hallucinates. A coroner that invents a cause of death isn't a coroner, it's a liar with nice handwriting. So between the model and the certificate there's a grounding gate . Before any eulogy or recovered summary reaches the card, I check that its claims trace back to the real evidence, the actual commit record, the real README. If the prose drifts into something the data doesn't support, the gate throws it out, and the certificate falls back to a strictly factual coroner that says so out loud. The tool would rather tell you "I couldn't ground this" than narrate a death it can't defend. That's not a bug I'm apologizing for, it's the feature. You can watch it hold the line across the three repos in the demo. bower/bower came back ABANDONED , and the differential is honest about its own doubt: abandoned 59%, burned_out 35%, completed 3%, pivoted 2%, alive basically nothing. It recovered "Bower is a package manager for the web," which is correct and plain. There were no defensible last words, so the death note stayed empty . It had nothing honest to quote, so it quoted nothing. Honestly, I think that blank space is the most trustworthy thing on the page. sindresorhus/caprine came back BURNED_OUT , and the recovered last words are almost too on the nose: "Caprine is feature complete." That's the maintainer, in their own README, signing their own certificate. It only shows up because it passed the grounding check against the real repo. I didn't write that line. The dead did. fastapi/fastapi came back a certificate of LIFE. Flatline still green. The coroner's just as willing to tell you a project's alive and you're the one who walked away. That reversal is the moment this stopped being a gimmick for me. It's not a death stamp, it reads the signal honestly either way. And since a tool about honesty can't go quiet in the one place honesty costs something, here's what it's not . The corpus is 117 rows, hand-labelled by me, so it's my little graveyard, not the universe of software. The six death modes are judgment calls; "burned out" vs "abandoned" is sometimes a story I'm choosing to tell about the numbers, and I believe the stories, but they're still stories. And it's slow on a cold case: a repo it's never seen means two live model calls plus a cold load, a couple of minutes, where a cached verdict comes back in under two seconds. I'd rather be honest and slow than fast and made up. None of that makes it useless. It makes it a forensic estimate that knows it's an estimate, which, for something stamping "cause of death" on your side projects, is exactly the posture I want. My graveyard's still full. The difference is every stone has a cause of death on it now, and I believe every one. Go autopsy your own. Paste your proudest dead repo and see how it died. Or find out, maybe a little uncomfortably, that it's still breathing and you're the one who walked away. Prize Categories Best Use of TabPFN. TabPFN is the beating heart of this project, not a bolt-on. It's the open-weight tabular foundation model behind every verdict, used the way Prior Labs recommends: as the core predictor inside a wider prediction system (feature extraction, LLM tie-breaking on the close calls, and a grounding gate around the output). And I did the thing the category actually asks for, measured it against a baseline on a real held-out test: 58.1% vs 43.6%, a 14.5-point win on leave-one-out across 117 repos.

fastapi/fastapi came back a certificate of LIFE. Flatline still green. The coroner's just as willing to tell you a project's alive and you're the one who walked away. That reversal is the moment this stopped being a gimmick for me. It's not a death stamp, it reads the signal honestly either way.

And since a tool about honesty can't go quiet in the one place honesty costs something, here's what it's not. The corpus is 117 rows, hand-labelled by me, so it's my little graveyard, not the universe of software. The six death modes are judgment calls; "burned out" vs "abandoned" is sometimes a story I'm choosing to tell about the numbers, and I believe the stories, but they're still stories. And it's slow on a cold case: a repo it's never seen means two live model calls plus a cold load, a couple of minutes, where a cached verdict comes back in under two seconds. I'd rather be honest and slow than fast and made up.

None of that makes it useless. It makes it a forensic estimate that knows it's an estimate, which, for something stamping "cause of death" on your side projects, is exactly the posture I want.

My graveyard's still full. The difference is every stone has a cause of death on it now, and I believe every one.

Go autopsy your own. Paste your proudest dead repo and see how it died. Or find out, maybe a little uncomfortably, that it's still breathing and you're the one who walked away.

Prize Categories

Best Use of TabPFN. TabPFN is the beating heart of this project, not a bolt-on. It's the open-weight tabular foundation model behind every verdict, used the way Prior Labs recommends: as the core predictor inside a wider prediction system (feature extraction, LLM tie-breaking on the close calls, and a grounding gate around the output). And I did the thing the category actually asks for, measured it against a baseline on a real held-out test: 58.1% vs 43.6%, a 14.5-point win on leave-one-out across 117 repos.

title: The Bengaluru Founder Building a Bridge to San Francisco
summary: Walk into any technology, AI or startup conference in Bengaluru , and you may encounter a familiar scene. Long queues around stalls handing out caps, water bottles, and T-shirts. Or some may gather around a well-known founder, hoping for a selfie and a video for Instagram Reels. In the crowd, a founder might as well be pitching a startup idea to an investor who might not be keen to listen at that hour. Amongst them, Suhas Motwani stands out, having built a vast network over seven years. Since 2019, he has built a community connecting product managers, founders, and tech leaders across India and the San Francisco Bay Area. In today's industry, access to the right network is paramount to shaping, funding, and scaling ideas. With that in mind, Motwani co-founded The Product Folks (TPF), a community of nearly 240,000 members, mostly product builders and managers worldwide. TPF partners with the leading product companies and startups of the world, and brings together founders and product builders across community meetups, workshops, dinners and mixers. It also offers education and mentorship from leading industry experts and product folks, including Shreyas Doshi, Lenny Rachitsky, Kunal Shah, and others who’ve made a significant impact in the sector. With 300+ community events and meetups a year across 35 cities, it brings together product leaders, managers, and founders under one roof. It also helps startups and companies hire product talent and helps Bay Area founders gauge India’s ecosystem, and vice versa. It has hosted community events around products and leaders from OpenAI, Replit, Lovable, Cursor and others. While it also offers paid courses and mentorship plans, most of its product guides, e-books, case studies, and teardowns are free, written by product leaders drawing on real-world experience. Paradoxically, as AI requires fewer humans, its advancement relies on them more than ever. Human ingenuity remains essential, with engineers refining AI safety, cost, and efficiency. Together, these talents drive Motwani’s mission. How TPF Was Born Over the past decade, India focused on building everyday apps, boasting developer talent but struggling with user acquisition and scaling. In simple terms, this is called ‘product management.’ Engineers struggled to scale when attempting to copy San Francisco's approach. Success required understanding user behaviour and designing engaging features. In 2019, while working at PepsiCo across business, product, and data, Motwani posted on social media to connect with others interested in product management. Expecting a small turnout at a Bengaluru WeWork room, sixty people attended. The response suggested demand for a space where people could learn from one another. Motwani says that before TPF was founded around 2015–16, most Indian product builders relied on lessons from Silicon Valley because local product management insights were scarce. The Bay Area’s product culture reached Bengaluru through Medium articles, Twitter posts, and Y Combinator lectures, but without human interaction, he says it still felt like a ‘black box.’ “We wanted to create a forum for people here who were interested in product management and needed a place to learn and share knowledge,” Motwani says. He was inspired by a free ProductTank workshop in London. Workshops attract attendees, but connections bring them back. Online resources couldn't replace direct insights from experienced builders, highlighting gaps in India's emerging product ecosystem. At the time, IT services dominated, and despite a vast developer pool, India lacked local benchmarks for acquiring users and scaling digital products. “We were fortunate to start when product management in India was still nascent. Companies such as Flipkart, Ola and Freecharge were growing, and their leaders had learned from people in the [Silicon] Valley before building their own organisations here,” says Motwani. Motwani realised that capital alone is insufficient for innovation. He felt experienced builders must collaborate. “We run over 300 annual events to democratise access, education, and learning,” says Motwani, who co-founded the effort with Aditya Mohanty, Abhay Jani, and Parth Batra. Nikhil Jois, growth lead at Bureau and an early TPF attendee, notes that events operate under ‘Chatham House’ rules. “Participants share candid experiences, mistakes, and lessons, offering a practical way to exchange notes among active builders.” Jois says this offers a different kind of learning than what you find online, where blogs and podcasts often present polished accounts of success rather than the messy realities of building a business. Over the years, TPF’s events and workshops have been made commercially viable through partnerships with companies. For startups, TPF offers more than brand visibility. Its events connect them directly with product managers, founders, and engineers who could become users, giving them a chance to demo features, gather feedback, and answer technical questions. They can also help companies gain traction in India. TPF recently hosted Café Cursor in Bengaluru, an informal meetup where developers bring their laptops and build alongside other Cursor users. After starting as pop-ups in San Francisco and New York, the format has expanded internationally, with TPF helping Cursor establish a presence in India. In another collaboration, TPF partnered with Replit for a hands-on build session where participants created applications using the platform. These gatherings also serve as product showcases, giving startups access to practitioners and a space to discuss technical features that may not attract mainstream media attention but matter to developers. TPF is also preparing for its flagship Un-Conference, which brings together product leaders from across the world. Passes range from ₹4,500 to ₹12,000. Throughout the year, it hosts free community meetups, where applicants can request an invite by outlining what they hope to learn and how they can contribute. As AI blurs the line between engineers, designers, and product managers, TPF is expanding its scope. As ChatGPT and Claude put a library of answers in front of people, people want to learn what someone learned the hard way more than ever. Meanwhile, Motwani and his team are helping Silicon Valley startups establish a presence in India. As companies look beyond the Bay Area, he believes entering the Indian market requires more than a local office. It demands access to the right ecosystem. “The Bay Area was dense and difficult to keep up with, so people were not thinking much about other places. That has begun to change as companies expand,” he says. “If companies lose market share in India now, catching up later may be difficult.” TPF aims to help companies navigate that transition, from deciding to enter India to building a meaningful presence. Recently, the community co-hosted a Bengaluru workshop for AI founders with OpenAI’s head of startups, Marc Manara , and others from the company. AIM attended the event, which focused on building AI products that can compete globally. Manara urged founders to maintain regular connections with the Bay Area, where much of the frontier AI research is taking place. “You just have to find the connectivity to be able to be in the loop of what’s happening.” That connectivity is now central to TPF’s next chapter: The Founder Folks (TFF), an initiative aimed at extending the community’s reach from product builders to founders. Building a Founder Matchmaking Service While TPF focuses on education and career development, The Founder Folks (TFF) helps people build companies. Motwani bets on a large pool of million-dollar businesses, not just a handful of billion-dollar startups. TFF facilitates targeted introductions for Indian founders entering the US market, where customers may be more willing to pay for AI products. Motwani believes a sustained effort over five to seven years could build a stronger corridor connecting founders, investors, customers and AI infrastructure across both regions. For some founders, these introductions have replaced months of cold outreach. Asad Abrar, founder of Drizz and a TFF member, says the community offers trusted advice on everything from product development to legal and taxation matters. “Finding trusted answers to all the questions you have on a daily basis is super critical as a founder,” he tells AIM. “TFF has brought a good curation of people where you can go ahead and share these questions and get relevant advice.” Chocolate Making Workshops for Series A Founders, and Golf Classes for CXOs With TFF, Motwani hopes to build another community once it reaches sufficient founder density. But he believes sustaining one requires more than putting people in a room. Communities must keep adapting to members’ interests and make participation worthwhile. “Communities need to keep listening to what people want. Many communities have disappeared; the hard part is adapting,” he says. Rather than relying on the usual panels, keynotes, and networking sessions, Motwani experiments with unconventional formats, from pickleball and venture capital meetups to supper clubs, CXO golf sessions, and chocolate-making workshops for Series A founders. TPF has also partnered with Bolna AI for a voice-themed pub quiz and hosted board game nights for founders. His larger ambition is to create a hundred communities like TPF to strengthen India's startup ecosystem. “India has built products in areas such as home services and ten-minute delivery, but we have not yet produced a consumer startup on the scale of Google or Meta. If even one such product came out of the TPF community, that would be a major achievement,” he says.
